title: Beyond the fear of death
hook: praising the One who ends all things loosens the fear of our own ending

segments.voice: Yesterday, des, every land, and your line, in every land. Today, a gentle day about the hardest subject there is.

There are plenty of ways of not thinking about it. People change the subject. They say passed away instead of died. They get through a funeral and go straight back to email. And then, at three in the morning, or in a hospital corridor, or on the anniversary of someone's going, the thought comes anyway: one day, me too. Traditions answer that three a.m. thought in different ways. Jaap Sahib answers it in a surprising way: not by talking about death less, but by naming the One who holds it.
screen: `WE CHANGE THE SUBJECT.` → `THE THREE A.M. THOUGHT.` → `JAAP NAMES WHO HOLDS IT.`

segments.voice: All through Jaap, the One is praised as the ender of all things. Sarab kaal. And one bhujang prayat line says namo kaal kaale: salutation to the death of death, the One who is the end even of endings. It might seem a grim thing to say every morning. But follow the logic. If death were a stranger, an enemy who could sneak up from outside, fear would make sense. Jaap says it isn't. Death isn't a rival power. It's in the One's hand, the same hand Jaap has called merciful, the house of compassion, the sustainer of all. In Jaap's picture, an ending isn't decided by a stranger; it's held by the One saluted every dawn. Some voices in Sikh scripture meet death almost gladly. Bhagat Kabir, whose words are in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that the death the whole world fears fills his mind with joy, because only through dying comes perfect, supreme bliss. Sikh teaching speaks of the soul returning to its source, like a drop to the ocean. That shapes how Sikhs mourn. At a Sikh funeral, people recite Kirtan Sohila, the bedtime prayer, and the Ardas. The Sikh code of conduct asks mourners not to wail or beat their chests, but to recite gurbani and remember Waheguru. Grief is real, and tears are human; no one is asked to pretend. But the hymns are recited anyway, because, as Sikhs see it, the one who has gone has gone home. In Jaap's picture, death is in his hand, and so is everyone death touches.
screen: `NAMO KAAL KAALE: DEATH OF DEATH.` · `NOT A STRANGER: IN THE ONE'S HAND.` · `KABIR: THE DEATH THE WORLD FEARS.` · `AT A FUNERAL, SOHILA AND ARDAS.` · then, large: `DEATH IS IN HIS HAND.`

segments.voice: Let your breath slow down, and notice that every out-breath is a small letting go, and every in-breath comes back without your asking. If someone you love has died, you can hold them gently in mind; if that's too heavy today, simply rest, hands open in your lap as if resting in larger hands. If you pray, you can say Waheguru.
Kaal. Time, and death — in Jaap, it is not a stranger but in the hand of the One praised as merciful, so fear can loosen.
Your line: death is in his hand. In Jaap, it is never a stranger's hand. Day three hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: At Sikh funerals, mourners recite Kirtan Sohila and the Ardas, and the Sikh code of conduct asks them to recite and remember rather than wail, understanding death as the soul's return to the One.

chat.says: Why would anyone praise the One as the death of death every morning? Isn't that grim?
options: In Jaap, death is no stranger; it's in the hand of the One praised as merciful.
It's meant to frighten people into praying harder before their time runs out.
It means Sikhs are told never to grieve, and to hide their tears at funerals.
chat.meaning: Namo kaal kaale bows to the death of death: an ending is held by the One Jaap calls merciful, not by a stranger.
